# Onboarding: your first hour with this kit

This copy is for Cursor. Type `/onboard` there and your agent shows it one step at a time; you can also read it all here.

## Step 1 of 8: Who this is for

People who want to use an AI coding agent on real projects, including people
who have never used one. The kit you installed gives you standing rules (in
Cursor Settings > Rules, if you pasted them there, or `AGENTS.md` in the repo you gave `--project`), three helper agents, a few commands and a commit check. This
walkthrough adds a first hour of practice: on your own repo, or on a demo if
you have none or want to test the install first.

It comes one step at a time. Each step ends with the command for the next one,
so you can stop whenever you like and pick up later. Ask your agent about
anything that is unclear, right there; that is usually faster than searching
the docs.

Next: type `/onboard 2` to go on.

## Step 2 of 8: Your plan

Your plan decides how fast you use up your limit, and so which rules tier fits
you. Your tool's own settings or docs say which plan you are on and where it
shows your usage.

- **A plan with a usage limit that resets:** stay on the starter tier, and use
  the `verifier` agent on work that matters rather than on every edit.
- **A larger plan with generous limits:** the full tier exists, but start on
  starter unless you already run several agents at once.
- **An API key, paid per token:** start on starter; the full tier's rules send
  more agents, and each one spends.

You chose the tier when you installed. To change it, run the installer again
with the other tier, adding the `--config-dir` or `--project` you used, if
any; `--dry-run` shows the plan and changes nothing:
- bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/install.py --tool cursor --tier full --dry-run`
- PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\install.py" --tool cursor --tier full --dry-run`

Next: type `/onboard 3` to go on.

## Step 3 of 8: The 5-minute mental model

Skip this if you have used your coding agent for a while; it is here as
reference. Your tool's docs give the exact keys and commands.

**Sessions.** Each time you start your agent in a folder, you start a session:
a conversation with that folder as its workspace. The agent can read files
there and, as your permissions allow, edit them and run commands. Starting a
new session gives it a fresh memory of the conversation.

**Rules files.** Plain text files of standing instructions the agent reads at
the start of every session. This kit's rules are in Cursor Settings > Rules, if you pasted them there, or `AGENTS.md` in the repo you gave `--project`.
Most tools also read an `AGENTS.md` at the root of a repo, for that repo alone.
This is where house rules go.

**Permissions.** Your tool decides, per action, whether the agent goes ahead,
asks you first, or never may. Keep edits and commands on asking until you
trust the agent in a repo.

**Commands.** Saved prompts you run by name. The kit's are
`/checkpoint`, `/lanes`, `/onboard` and `/starter-update`.

**Subagents.** A separate agent with its own context, sent to do one job and
report back. The kit adds three: `verifier`, `code-reviewer` and `consultant`.
You call one by asking, for example "use the verifier agent to check this".

**Skills.** Checklists the agent loads only when the work matches, such as the
kit's backend and frontend guardrails.

**Context.** Everything in the session (your messages, files read, command
output) shares one context window. When it fills, older detail gets summarised
or dropped. Start a fresh session when you switch to an unrelated task, so
stale detail does not crowd out what matters now.

**Usage.** Long sessions, large files, bigger models and many subagents all
spend faster, on a plan's limit or on your API bill.

Next: type `/onboard 4` to go on.

## Step 4 of 8: How this kit works

The rules ask your agent to work like this:

- **Classify the task first:** say whether it is a spike, a change to something
  that exists, or new architecture, because each needs a different amount of
  care.
- **Root cause before fix:** a fix for a bug you do not understand is a guess,
  and three failed fixes means the design is wrong.
- **Verify independently:** the agent that did the work does not get to declare
  it done; another one re-runs the checks.
- **Say what you ran versus what you reasoned:** "tests pass" means they ran and
  someone read the output, and commits record which is which.
- **Simplest thing first:** no new dependency or service without evidence it is
  needed, built so the bigger option can replace it later.
- **Confirm before anything outward-facing:** pushes, deploys, messages and
  deletes wait for your yes, because git cannot undo them.

Each rule is written down with the reason it exists, in Cursor Settings > Rules, if you pasted them there, or `AGENTS.md` in the repo you gave `--project`.
Keep a rule only while you can say what failure it prevents.

## Step 5 of 8: What you got

The kit's rules are in Cursor Settings > Rules, if you pasted them there, or `AGENTS.md` in the repo you gave `--project`. The installer added the agents,
commands and skills below, and backed up every file it changed.

| Piece | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `/checkpoint` | After a change: runs the relevant checks, says what ran and what did not, proposes a commit message, waits for your yes |
| `verifier` agent | Re-runs build and tests on work reported as done, without editing anything |
| `code-reviewer` agent | Reviews a diff for the ways this project breaks (money, auth, time, data), not style |
| `consultant` agent | Answers a question about another part of the codebase so your session does not have to read it all |
| `/lanes` | Splits a repo with several stacks (say, a frontend and a backend) into lanes |
| `/starter-update` | Updates the kit: shows the plan, applies nothing until you say yes |
| Guardrail skills | Checks while writing endpoints, UI, data jobs and code that calls a model |
| Commit guard | In repos you gave the installer with `--guard-repo`: checks commits for secrets, personal data and a `Verified:` or `Unverified:` line |

The agents are read-only by instruction; where your tool can enforce it, the
installer set that too, and its closing message said which. To add the commit
guard to a repo, run the installer again with `--guard-repo`, using the tier
you installed and any `--config-dir` or `--project` you used; `--dry-run`
changes nothing:
- bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/install.py --tool cursor --tier starter --guard-repo <your-repo> --dry-run`
- PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\install.py" --tool cursor --tier starter --guard-repo <your-repo> --dry-run`

Next: type `/onboard 6` to go on.

## Step 6 of 8: Try it on a demo

Skip this step if you have a repo of your own to practise on: the next step
uses it. If you have none, or want to see the whole chain work before you trust
the kit with your code, try a demo. A demo is a small project your agent builds
in a new folder from a brief, graded by held-out checks kept in the kit, not in
that folder.

1. **Pick one.** Run this in a terminal, or ask your agent to run it. It asks
   what you want to spend, then lists the demos with what each costs on your
   plan where that has been measured, and says so where it has not:
   - bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/starter.py demo pick --tool cursor`
   - PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\starter.py" demo pick --tool cursor`
2. **Start it.** The same launcher with `demo start <name> --tool cursor`
   makes the folder `~/agent-demos/<name>`: a git repo whose commits the commit
   guard's git hooks check. It prints how to open a session there and what to
   type first.
3. **Watch the chain** in that new session: a plan, the build, its tests, the
   `verifier` agent, `/checkpoint`, then a commit, which the demo's own
   commit guard hooks check. To grade the work yourself, run the launcher's
   `demo check <name>` line that the start step printed, not `npm test`, which
   the agent can change. It ends with `PASS` or `FAIL`. Like any grade made on
   your machine, it is feedback, not proof: the agent has a shell there too.
   A measured run counts only after the kit's CI re-grades the committed
   folder.

Deleting the folder undoes the demo, and nothing in it leaves your machine
unless you push it yourself.

Next: type `/onboard 7` to go on.

## Step 7 of 8: Your first hour

Do this in a repo of your own with a clean `git status`. Make a branch first so
nothing lands on your main branch by accident.

1. **Open it.** Start your agent in the repo's folder.
2. **Give the repo its own rules.** If your tool has a command that drafts a
   rules file by reading the repo, run it; otherwise ask the agent to write an
   `AGENTS.md` that says how to run the tests, what the project is and what
   must never break. Read it and correct anything wrong. This file is worth
   more than any prompt you will type.
3. **Ask for a small change.** Pick something real and small: a confusing
   function to tidy, a missing test, a bug you already understand. Notice that
   the agent says how it classifies the task before it starts. If it guesses
   wrong, say so.
4. **Run `/checkpoint`.** It runs the checks that cover the change, tells
   you what it did not run, shows the diff and proposes a commit message with
   a `Verified:` or `Unverified:` line. It stops and waits for you.
5. **Ask for an independent check.** Type something like: "Use the verifier
   agent to check that this change works." Compare its report with what the
   session claimed. Any gap between the two is the point of the exercise.
6. **Commit, if you are happy.** Approve the commit. Where the commit guard is
   installed, read any warning it gives and decide whether it is real.

Next: type `/onboard 8` to go on.

## Step 8 of 8: Where to go next

- **Graduate to full:** once you regularly run several agents at once, install
  the full tier. It adds rules for picking a model and effort level per task
  and for coordinating agents. `--dry-run` shows the plan first; add the
  `--config-dir` or `--project` you used, if any:
  - bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/install.py --tool cursor --tier full --dry-run`
  - PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\install.py" --tool cursor --tier full --dry-run`
- **Pick models per role:** `MODELS.md` in the kit says which role each agent
  plays. Map those roles to models your tool offers.
- **A repo with two stacks:** run `/lanes` once in it.
- **Make the rules yours:** edit your rules file, outside the block marked
  `BEGIN claude-starter rules`; an update replaces that block. Keep a rule only
  while you can say what failure it prevents.
- **Keep it current:** `/starter-update` shows what a new release changes
  and applies nothing until you say yes.
- **Something misbehaved:** if the commit guard flags something it should not,
  or an agent or skill from this kit does something wrong, run this in a
  terminal. It saves a redacted report and sends nothing unless you add
  `--submit` and confirm (`--kind` can also be `agent-misbehaved`):
  - bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/report.py --kind guard-false-positive --tool cursor --step "what happened"`
  - PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\report.py" --kind guard-false-positive --tool cursor --step "what happened"`

That was the last step. Next: after your next change, type `/checkpoint`.
